title: Long-Term Melatonin Use and Heart Failure Risk
hook: Chronic-insomnia patients on long-term melatonin had roughly 90% higher heart failure risk over five years — an association, not proof, but a reason to stop assuming it is harmless.
key_points: A large preliminary study followed people with chronic insomnia who used melatonin long term.
Long-term users had about a 90% higher risk of developing heart failure over five years.
This is an association study — it does not show melatonin causes heart problems.
People with chronic insomnia already carry extra cardiovascular risk, which is hard to fully separate out.
Melatonin is sold as a supplement, so it gets far less long-term safety scrutiny than a prescription drug.
Short-term use for jet lag or shifted schedules is a different question from nightly use for years.
content_html: Melatonin has a reputation as the harmless sleep aid: it's a hormone your body already makes, you can buy it at any pharmacy, and nobody calls it a drug. A large preliminary study complicates that picture. Among people with chronic insomnia, those who used melatonin long term had roughly a 90% higher risk of developing heart failure over five years.
extra_html:
The caveats matter. This is observational research, so it can show that long-term melatonin use and heart failure travel together without showing that one causes the other. People who reach for melatonin night after night tend to be people with entrenched insomnia — and chronic insomnia is itself linked to cardiovascular disease. Untangling the supplement from the condition it's treating is exactly the kind of problem this study design can't fully solve.

What the finding does puncture is the assumption that melatonin needs no thought at all. Because it's regulated as a supplement, it has never faced the long-term safety testing a prescription sleep drug would. If you've been taking it nightly for years, that's worth raising with a clinician — and worth treating persistent insomnia as a condition to address rather than something to paper over indefinitely.

related.title: When Sleep Problems Need Help
related.hook: Better sleep habits fix a lot — but not everything. Loud snoring with gasping, or weeks of being unable to sleep, are signals to see a doctor, not push through.

related.title: Building Better Sleep Habits
related.hook: Good sleep is mostly built in the hours before bed. A handful of simple habits — collectively called sleep hygiene — do more than any gadget.

related.title: A $70 Billion Industry With Thin Evidence
related.hook: Supplements are one of the fastest-growing corners of health spending. For most of what's on the shelf, there's little evidence it does what the label implies.

related.title: Taking Medicines Safely
related.hook: Medicines help only when used right. Most medication mishaps are preventable with a few habits — reading the label, knowing your list, and asking questions.

flashcards.prompt: What did the melatonin study actually find?

choices.text: An association: long-term users had ~90% higher heart failure risk over five years
Proof that melatonin damages the heart muscle
That melatonin protects against heart failure

flashcards.explanation_html: It was a large preliminary observational study. A 90% higher risk is a strong signal, but association is not causation — chronic insomnia itself raises cardiovascular risk.

flashcards.prompt: Why does melatonin get less safety scrutiny than a sleeping pill you'd be prescribed?
flashcards.back_html: It's sold as a supplement, not a drug, so it never went through the long-term safety testing prescription sleep medications face. "Natural" and "over the counter" are not evidence of long-term safety.

flashcards.prompt: What's the practical takeaway if you take melatonin every night?
flashcards.back_html: Worth a conversation with a clinician. Occasional short-term use for jet lag is a different situation from years of nightly use — and chronic insomnia itself deserves treatment beyond a supplement.
